client: I've been dreading something that's coming up next month, and it's been eating at me more than I expected. There's a family reunion, and every time we have one, my cousin makes these comments about my career in front of everyone, like I'm some kind of cautionary tale. I honestly don't even know if talking about it will change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like this reunion carries a lot of weight for you — being publicly called out by your cousin in front of family isn't just uncomfortable, it can feel genuinely humiliating, and it makes sense that it's been sitting with you. I also notice you mentioned not being sure talking will help, and I'm curious about that — has it felt like nothing changes no matter what you do, or is there something specific that's made it hard to imagine things being different?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, it's more like... no matter how many times I go over it in my head, I still end up feeling like I did something wrong, even though I know logically I didn't deserve to be called out like that in front of everyone. It's like my brain just keeps circling back to the same place — shame, I guess — and talking about it hasn't really moved that needle before. I've vented to a friend about it and felt better for like an hour, and then it all came rushing back, so I guess I'm skeptical that this will be any different.
therapist: That loop you're describing — where your logic and your gut just won't agree — is actually really common with shame, because shame lives deeper than reasoning and doesn't budge just from venting. What you're pointing to is exactly why we'd want to do something different here: not just talk *about* the feeling, but gently examine the belief underneath it, like what it would mean about you if your cousin's comments were actually true. What do you think that story is — the one your brain keeps landing on when it circles back to shame?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think the story is something like... I'm fundamentally not enough, like no matter how hard I try, I'm always going to fall short of what people expect from me. And my cousin's comments just kind of confirmed what I already suspected about myself, which is maybe why they hit so hard. It's embarrassing to even say that out loud, because part of me knows it sounds irrational, but another part of me is like, well, what if it's actually true?
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and the fact that it felt embarrassing to say out loud tells me this belief has been quietly carrying a lot of weight for a long time. That "what if it's true" question is actually the heart of what we'd want to explore together — not to argue you out of it, but to really look at the evidence your mind is using to keep that story alive. Can you think of a time, even a small one, where the story of "not enough" didn't quite fit what actually happened?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I guess there was this one time at work where I actually solved a problem that my whole team had been stuck on for days, and my manager specifically called me out in front of everyone for it. But even as I'm saying it, my brain is already doing this thing where it's like, "yeah but that was just luck" or "they would have figured it out without you eventually." It's like no matter what example I come up with, there's always this automatic voice ready to tear it down before it even has a chance to mean anything.
therapist: You just did something really important — you found real evidence against that "not enough" story, and then watched your mind immediately move the goalposts, which is actually a classic pattern called a cognitive distortion called "discounting the positive." I'm also noticing you shared that pretty quickly, like you were almost rushing past it before it could land — I wonder if there's something uncomfortable about actually letting that moment at work count for something? What would it mean for you if you allowed yourself to take that win seriously, even just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... I guess if I actually let it count, it would feel good for a second, but then it's like, what if that's the one time I get it right and everything after that just proves I'm not? It's almost safer to not get too attached to it, you know? Like I'm protecting myself from being disappointed later when I inevitably mess something up at work again.
therapist: What you just described is actually a really sophisticated protective strategy — your mind has learned that hope feels dangerous, so it's easier to stay in the low expectations lane than to risk the drop. But I want to gently point out the cost of that protection: it means the "not enough" story never gets a fair trial, because any evidence against it gets dismissed before it can stick. What do you think it would feel like to let one piece of good evidence actually stay, just as an experiment, without needing it to prove anything about the future?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it logically, like I can follow the reasoning. But when you ask what it would feel like to let good evidence "stay," I honestly don't know, because the moment something good happens, there's this immediate voice that says "yeah, but that's just one time" or "they were just being polite." It's like the good stuff has to pass this impossible test before I'll even consider it real, and I'm not sure I trust myself to run that experiment fairly.
therapist: The way you described that "impossible test" is really striking — it's like you've set up a system where good things have to prove themselves beyond any reasonable doubt, but the "not enough" story gets to walk in without showing any ID at all. And I notice you said you don't trust yourself to run the experiment fairly, which might actually be the most important thing you've said today — because that distrust of your own judgment is part of the same story. What do you think it would take for you to start trusting yourself as a fair witness to your own life, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Because I don't even know what a fair witness to my own life would look like — I think I've been so used to being my own harshest critic that "fair" feels almost foreign, like I wouldn't recognize it if it showed up. And part of me wonders if trusting my own judgment is even safe, because what if I'm just fooling myself into thinking things are okay when they're not?
therapist: The way you're sitting with that question — really letting it land rather than deflecting — tells me something important is shifting, even if it doesn't feel that way yet. I want to offer a gentle reframe: being a fair witness doesn't mean lowering your guard or fooling yourself, it actually means applying the same standard to good evidence that you already apply to bad — rigorous, not lenient. What if "fair" wasn't the opposite of critical, but just meant your wins and your stumbles both had to show the same ID at the door?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That metaphor actually caught me off guard a little — "showing the same ID at the door." I think I understand what you're saying, but honestly my gut reaction is that I've spent so long using self-criticism as a way to stay safe, like if I beat myself up first then nothing can blindside me, so the idea of letting good evidence in with the same rigor feels almost... dangerous? Like I'm worried that if I start acknowledging wins, I'll get complacent and then something will go wrong and I won't have seen it coming.
therapist: What you're describing is actually one of the most common ways shame protects itself — by convincing you that self-criticism is a survival tool, not a burden, so giving it up feels like walking into traffic. But here's what's worth examining: has the self-criticism actually prevented bad things from happening, or has it mainly just made the waiting feel more controlled? I'm curious whether you can think of a time something went wrong *despite* you having already beaten yourself up about it in advance.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Yeah, I can actually think of something right away — I spent weeks tearing myself apart before a big presentation at work, convinced that if I just criticized myself enough I'd somehow perform better, and it still went badly. So I guess the self-criticism didn't actually protect me from anything. But honestly, even hearing myself say that, there's this voice that immediately jumps in and says "well, maybe it would have been even worse if you hadn't been hard on yourself," and I can't really argue with that thought, it just feels true even when I know it probably isn't.
therapist: You just cracked something open — you found a real-world test case where the self-criticism failed to do its one job, and your mind's response was to immediately invent an unfalsifiable defense, "it would have been even worse." That's actually a sign of how hard that belief is working to survive, because an argument that can never be proven wrong is one that never has to be. What do you notice happens in your body when you sit with the possibility that the self-criticism just... didn't help, full stop?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I notice my chest gets kind of tight, and there's this urge to look away or change the subject, like my brain is genuinely uncomfortable just sitting with that idea. It's almost like if I admit the self-criticism didn't help, then I wasted all that suffering for nothing, and that feels worse somehow. I don't know if that makes sense, but letting go of it feels scarier than keeping it.
therapist: What you just described makes complete sense — if the suffering had a purpose, it wasn't wasted, but if it didn't help, then you carried all of that for nothing, and that's a genuinely painful thing to face. That tight chest and urge to look away is your mind trying to protect you from that grief, which is real and worth acknowledging. What if the goal wasn't to decide whether the suffering was wasted, but just to ask: do you want to keep paying that cost going forward?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
